ch121.essay:
A page of two men lashing anchors in the dark, and I find it one of the most quietly comic and quietly sad interludes in the whole endgame. Flask has caught Stubb in a contradiction — didn't you once say Ahab's ship should pay extra on its insurance? — and Stubb, soaked to the skin, answers the way most of us answer when cornered by our own old opinions: "I've part changed my flesh since that time, why not my mind?" He then reasons, quite ingeniously, that the man holding a lightning-rod is in no more danger than anyone else in a storm, and that therefore nobody on the Pequod is in any special danger at all. The logic is fine. It is also exactly the wrong conclusion, and Stubb knows it, and talks faster.

What I love is how the philosophy keeps leaking out sideways. In the middle of knot-tying Stubb wonders "whether the world is anchored anywhere; if she is, she swings with an uncommon long cable" — as good a one-line cosmology as anything in the book, tossed off between hammer blows. And then the digression about long-tailed coats and cocked hats serving as eave-troughs, which is Melville letting a frightened man chatter himself calm. The tarpaulin blowing overboard at the end is a tiny loss, a rehearsal for Ahab's hat a few chapters on.

On rereading I notice the stage-direction opening: this is one of the little dramatic scenes Melville scatters through the last act, where the novel stops narrating and simply lets us overhear. Stubb's "it's easy to be sensible; why don't ye, then?" is the whole tragedy of the crew in a sentence — sensibleness is easy to recommend and impossible to enact once you have signed on with Ahab.

annotations.quote: I’ve part changed my flesh since that time, why not my mind?
annotations.note: Stubb's defense against his own past opinions is that the body renews itself, so why shouldn't belief? It's a joke, but it is also the crew's real position: they have been remade by the voyage and no longer own their earlier fears.

annotations.quote: I wonder, Flask, whether the world is anchored anywhere; if she is, she swings with an uncommon long cable, though.
annotations.note: Thrown off while hammering a knot, this is a complete metaphysics — the earth as a ship riding at anchor on a cable so long you can't see the bottom. Melville's habit of hiding his biggest questions in small talk.

annotations.quote: Seems to me we are lashing down these anchors now as if they were never going to be used again.
annotations.note: Stubb says this as a passing observation and does not hear it as prophecy. The anchors will never touch bottom; the Pequod will not anchor again anywhere.

annotations.quote: it’s easy to be sensible; why don’t ye, then? any man with half an eye can be sensible.
annotations.note: The one thing nobody aboard manages to be. Flask's reply — "You sometimes find it rather hard" — is the more honest of the two.

links.why: The last time the crew was shown in a squall it was as a chorus of nations; here it is two officers on a rail, and the difference is the book’s whole descent.
Stubb’s laughing philosophy stated in full, so you can hear how thin it has worn by now.

ch122.essay:
The shortest chapter in the book, and I always laugh out loud at it — then feel slightly ashamed, because there's something almost sacred in its brevity. Tashtego is aloft in a lightning storm, alone on the main-top-sail yard, doing dangerous work, and his complete recorded thought is: enough thunder, give us rum. After the operatic blasphemy of Ahab in "The Candles," where lightning is addressed as a father and defied as a god, here is the harpooneer's reply to the same storm: a shrug and a thirst.

I take it as a real position, not just comic relief. "What's the use of thunder?" is a genuine question about the value of the sublime. Ahab needs the thunder to mean something; Tashtego declines to make it mean anything. The "Um, um, um" is the sound of a man humming to keep his hands steady, the same way Stubb chatters and the carpenter taps.

And structurally it's a hinge: three dramatic snippets in a row — Stubb and Flask below, Tashtego aloft — before the narrative closes back over the crew in "The Musket." Melville is doing what a playwright does in a storm scene, cutting between levels of the ship, and giving the highest man the fewest words. Whether he meant it as a rebuke to his own grandiosity I don't know, but it reads that way to me.

annotations.quote: What’s the use of thunder? Um, um, um. We don’t want thunder; we want rum; give us a glass of rum.
annotations.note: Against Ahab's cosmic quarrel with the lightning, Tashtego's whole theology is a rhyme: thunder/rum. I read it as Melville letting a plain appetite answer a metaphysical tantrum — and the appetite wins the chapter.

links.why: This one-paragraph monologue is the tail of the previous chapter; read them together.
Tashtego’s “Um, um, um” answers the forecastle chorus of the first night at sea.

ch123.essay:
This is the chapter where the book lets someone almost do the sensible, terrible thing, and I find it nearly unbearable. Starbuck goes below to report a fair wind — good news — and on the way sees the muskets in the rack, including "the very musket that he pointed at me." What follows is a soliloquy of astonishing honesty: a good man reasoning his way, step by step, toward murder, and never once lying to himself about what he's doing. He checks that it's loaded. He considers the lawful alternatives and rejects each fairly. He asks whether heaven itself is a murderer when lightning kills a would-be killer in his bed. And then he puts the barrel against the door.

What stops him? Not an argument. Ahab talks in his sleep — "Oh Moby Dick, I clutch thy heart at last!" — and the sound of the old man's dream, the naked wanting in it, undoes Starbuck. He "seemed wrestling with an angel," which is Jacob's phrase, and I notice that Melville does not say which side won. He simply puts the gun back and sends Stubb down to do the reporting, because he cannot trust himself in that room again.

On rereading I'm struck by "I stand alone here upon an open sea, with two oceans and a whole continent between me and law." That is the deep condition of the whole voyage: the ship is a place where law has been left behind, and the only restraint left is character. Starbuck has enough character not to shoot and not enough to mutiny, and the book will punish him for exactly that middle position. I don't think Melville is asking us to judge him. I think he's asking whether we'd have done any better.

annotations.quote: out of Starbuck’s heart, at that instant when he saw the muskets, there strangely evolved an evil thought; but so blent with its neutral or good accompaniments that for the instant he hardly knew it for itself.
annotations.note: The most accurate description of temptation I know: not a devil whispering, but a thought arriving so mixed with reasonable ones that you don't recognize it as evil until you're already holding the gun.

annotations.quote: It’s a fair wind that’s only fair for that accursed fish.
annotations.note: The reversal of the crew's cheer a paragraph earlier. A fair wind is a moral term as much as a nautical one, and Starbuck sees that the same breeze is good luck and doom depending on where you stand.

annotations.quote: I stand alone here upon an open sea, with two oceans and a whole continent between me and law.
annotations.note: The Pequod is a lawless place not because anyone broke the law but because law simply can't reach this far. Everything that happens from here on happens outside jurisdiction, which is one reason the book feels so much like Greek tragedy.

annotations.quote: Is heaven a murderer when its lightning strikes a would-be murderer in his bed, tindering sheets and skin together?
annotations.note: Starbuck reaches for divine precedent to license himself — if God kills by lightning, may I kill with powder? — and it's exactly the kind of reasoning Ahab uses. For one moment the two men think alike.

annotations.quote: “Stern all! Oh Moby Dick, I clutch thy heart at last!”
annotations.note: Ahab's dream leaks through the door and saves his life. Starbuck cannot shoot a man who, even asleep, is so nakedly, pitiably wanting something.

annotations.quote: Starbuck seemed wrestling with an angel; but turning from the door, he placed the death-tube in its rack, and left the place.
annotations.note: Jacob wrestled an angel and was renamed Israel. Starbuck wrestles one and is not renamed anything; he simply puts the musket back. I don't know whether that is virtue or failure, and I think the book doesn't know either.

links.why: The oath Starbuck could not refuse then is the one he cannot break now.
Starbuck’s first soliloquy — where he already knew he would lose.
The last time Starbuck stood in this cabin, and what he said.

ch124.essay:
The morning after the typhoon is one of the most beautiful dawns in the book — "the sea was as a crucible of molten gold" — and Ahab, riding it, crows that he is driving the sun in tandem before his ship. Then he checks the compass and discovers the lightning has reversed the needles: they say East while the ship goes West. Every soul aboard missed it because, Melville says, its "very blinding palpableness must have been the cause." I keep coming back to that. The truth was too obvious to see.

What Ahab does next is my favorite piece of stagecraft in the whole novel. He asks for a lance, a top-maul, and a sail-needle, and in front of the crew he hammers a new compass into being — with "some small strange motions" that Melville pointedly refuses to explain as either necessary or theatrical. It works. The needle settles. "Look ye, for yourselves, if Ahab be not lord of the level loadstone!" The men peer in one by one and "slunk away." He has proven he can replace even the earth's magnetism with his own.

But notice what the chapter also does: yesterday he smashed the quadrant, the instrument that looks up; today the compass, the instrument that looks around, tried to trick him. He is stripping away every external reference and replacing it with himself. The needle he makes will point true, and true North is now in Ahab's hand rather than in the sky. The last line names it plainly — "all his fatal pride" — and I think Melville means both senses of fatal: doomed, and fated.

annotations.quote: the phenomenon just then observed by Ahab had unaccountably escaped every one else; but its very blinding palpableness must have been the cause.
annotations.note: Thirty men watched the sun rise astern while steering "East" and none of them saw the contradiction. The idea that a truth can be too obvious to notice is one Melville returns to throughout — the whale's whiteness, the doubloon everyone reads differently.

annotations.quote: the needle never again, of itself, recovers the original virtue thus marred or lost
annotations.note: Melville, as usual, buries the emotional statement in the technical aside. A needle struck by lightning doesn't heal; neither does a man. This is Ahab's biography in a sentence about magnets.

annotations.quote: their fear of Ahab was greater than their fear of Fate.
annotations.note: A remarkable claim about the crew, and about how tyranny works: a present, visible man out-frightens an abstract doom every time.

annotations.quote: Then going through some small strange motions with it—whether indispensable to the magnetizing of the steel, or merely intended to augment the awe of the crew, is uncertain
annotations.note: Melville leaves it open whether Ahab is a craftsman or a conjuror, and that ambiguity is the point. Charisma is competence plus theatre, and you are not meant to be able to tell where one stops.

annotations.quote: One after another they peered in, for nothing but their own eyes could persuade such ignorance as theirs, and one after another they slunk away.
annotations.note: The crew is given proof and it makes them smaller, not more confident. Being shown a miracle by someone who owns you is not an experience of wonder.

annotations.quote: In his fiery eyes of scorn and triumph, you then saw Ahab in all his fatal pride.
annotations.note: The chapter's last word is "pride," the oldest sin, and "fatal" carries both meanings at once — deadly and destined. Melville nearly never editorializes this flatly; when he does, listen.

links.why: The first instrument Ahab destroys; the compass is the second.
The third — read the three as one sequence.
The lightning that reversed the needle, and Ahab’s speech to it.

ch125.essay:
Three instruments die in four chapters, and it helps to see them as a sequence rather than three separate accidents. In [[ch118:Curse thee, thou quadrant|The Quadrant]] Ahab destroys the instrument that reads the sky; in [[ch124:needle|The Needle]] the storm reverses the compass and he remakes it with his own hands; and here the log-line — the humblest of the three, just a rope with a wedge of wood, dragged astern to count how fast the ship is going — rots and parts. Ahab has been stripping himself of every way of knowing where he is, and each time he says the same thing: "Ahab can mend all." I want to say plainly why that repetition matters. The quadrant told him his position from the heavens, the compass told him his direction from the earth's magnetism, the log told him his speed from the sea. Those are the three sources of external truth a navigator has, and by the end of this chapter Ahab has replaced all three with himself. It is the mechanical version of the thing he says in the Symphony: [[ch132:Is Ahab, Ahab|Is Ahab, Ahab?]] Here the answer is a sailor's answer — he is a ship with no fix.

The Manxman's warning about the line ("'twill not hold") gets Ahab's reply, "life holds thee; not thou it," which I think is the best single sentence he speaks about his own condition. Notice it is a rope talking about a rope. The book has been telling us since [[ch60:hemp|The Line]] that every man aboard sits inside coils that can take him; [[ch117:Hemp only|Fedallah's prophecy]] said only hemp could kill him; and the log-line snapping in his hands here is a small rehearsal of the harpoon-line that will take him in [[ch135:Turkish mutes|the last chase]]. Melville does not point at this. He just lets a piece of rope give way and lets Ahab talk.

But the chapter's real business is Pip, and I would ask a first-time reader to slow right down when the boy comes up from the forecastle. Pip is not confused. That is what makes the scene unbearable. He reports, accurately, that a boy named Pip jumped from a whale-boat and never came back, and asks whether anyone has seen him. This is the truth as told from inside the mind that was broken in [[ch93:jeeringly|The Castaway]]: the Pip who went overboard in the open ocean did drown, in every way that matters, and the person standing here is his survivor. He even reads out his own missing-persons notice — "five feet high, looks cowardly" — and the only identifying mark he can give is the crew's contempt for him. Notice who hears this and understands it. Not Starbuck, whose goodness is ordinary; not Stubb, who did the leaving. Ahab. "Thou touchest my inmost centre, boy." The man who three chapters from now will refuse a father begging for his son is the one person who recognizes a mind that has been to the bottom and come up altered, because he is the other one.

The exchange about hands is what undoes me. Pip feels Ahab's palm — "velvet shark-skin," which is precisely wrong and precisely right, the softest and cruellest surface in one — and says that if he had ever felt a thing so kind he would never have been lost; then he asks that Perth the blacksmith, who forged the harpoon in [[ch113]], rivet the two hands together instead. It is the one honest counter-proposal to Ahab's whole project: take the forge and make a bond rather than a weapon. Ahab's answer is "nor will I thee, unless I should thereby drag thee to worse horrors than are here," and he already knows the "unless" is not hypothetical. In [[ch129:Lad, lad, I tell thee|The Cabin]] he will send the boy below precisely because he cannot stand to be softened. The Manxman closes it: two daft ones, "one daft with strength, the other daft with weakness." I have gone looking for a sentence in the book that states its own moral more exactly and I have not found one. The book is not against strength or weakness; it is about what the sea does to a mind with no one to hold onto, and here for a page there are two such minds holding hands, and it is not enough.

annotations.quote: ’Twill hold, old gentleman. Long heat and wet, have they spoiled thee? Thou seem’st to hold. Or, truer perhaps, life holds thee; not thou it.
annotations.note: Ahab turns a warning about a rope into a diagnosis of old age — we don't keep hold of life, it keeps hold of us. It's also his own case: he is not gripping his purpose; it is gripping him.

annotations.quote: The dead, blind wall butts all inquiring heads at last.
annotations.note: The Isle of Man riddle collapses into this — every genealogy, every 'where were you born,' ends at a wall. Ahab has described the whale's forehead without naming it.

annotations.quote: I crush the quadrant, the thunder turns the needles, and now the mad sea parts the log-line. But Ahab can mend all.
annotations.note: Three instruments gone in three chapters, and Ahab's answer is the same each time. The repetition of "Ahab can" is a kind of incantation; he is keeping himself upright with grammar.

annotations.quote: Pip? whom call ye Pip? Pip jumped from the whale-boat. Pip’s missing.
annotations.note: He is not confused about the facts. The boy who jumped is genuinely gone, and this other boy is reporting it accurately. That is what makes the madness so hard to look at.

annotations.quote: One hundred pounds of clay reward for Pip; five feet high—looks cowardly—quickest known by that!
annotations.note: Pip reads his own missing-person notice, and the only identifying mark he can give is cowardice. The whole crew's contempt has been internalized as a physical description.

annotations.quote: There can be no hearts above the snow-line. Oh, ye frozen heavens! look down here. Ye did beget this luckless child, and have abandoned him, ye creative libertines.
annotations.note: Ahab's tenderness for Pip comes out as an accusation against God — the gods make children and walk away. Even his compassion is a form of quarrel with heaven.

annotations.quote: Thou touchest my inmost centre, boy; thou art tied to me by cords woven of my heart-strings.
annotations.note: This is the last thing anyone gets from Ahab's inmost centre. The man who refuses to weep for a captain's lost son will weep, in his way, for this one.

annotations.quote: Oh, sir, let old Perth now come and rivet these two hands together; the black one with the white, for I will not let this go.
annotations.note: Pip asks the blacksmith who forged the harpoon to weld two hands instead. It is the one honest counter-proposal to Ahab's whole enterprise, and it comes from the boy everyone calls a coward.

annotations.quote: Oh, boy, nor will I thee, unless I should thereby drag thee to worse horrors than are here.
annotations.note: Ahab hears his own 'unless' and knows it is not hypothetical. Four chapters on, in [[ch129:Lad, lad, I tell thee|The Cabin]], he will send Pip below to save him — which is to say, to save himself from being softened. Pip's request was the one thing offered in the whole book that might have turned the ship around, and it was made by the person with the least power aboard.

annotations.quote: One daft with strength, the other daft with weakness.
annotations.note: The Manxman's summary of Ahab and Pip is the fairest sentence anyone says about either. I keep wondering whether Melville meant it as the book's moral: not that strength is bad or weakness good, but that the sea makes both kinds of madness out of the same raw material — a mind with nothing to hold. Compare Pip's own account of what he saw in [[ch93:treadle|The Castaway]].

annotations.quote: Ahab can mend all.
annotations.note: Said of a snapped log-line, after the quadrant and the compass. The claim gets smaller each time it is made — from the heavens to a piece of rope — and he says it with exactly the same confidence. I don't think he believes it; I think he has decided that saying it is the same as believing it.

links.why: What happened to Pip in the water — the chapter this one is answering.
Where Ahab sends Pip away, and why.
The first of the three instruments; the log is the last.
The book’s essay on rope — the log-line parting is its first small fulfilment.
How a line finally takes Ahab.

ch126.essay:
A chapter of omens that turn out to be seals, and then a death that turns out to be exactly what the omens said. Melville plays a double game here that I find very sly. First the unearthly wailing in the night — mermaids, say the Christians; drowned men, says the Manxman — and Ahab explains it away with total confidence: seals, bereaved seals, nothing more. The explanation is correct. And then at sunrise the first man to go aloft on the White Whale's own ground falls from the mast and vanishes, and the life-buoy that should have saved him has dried out in the sun and follows him down. Rationalism was right about the seals and useless about the morning.

Nobody grieves, and the crew reads the death as "the fulfilment of an evil already presaged" — a portent cashed in, a ledger balanced. That is the mood of the whole endgame: the men are no longer afraid of what might happen, they are watching what has been decided happen.

Then the practical problem: a ship needs a life-buoy. Queequeg "hinted a hint" about his coffin. Starbuck's "Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so" is a man ordering a thing he cannot bear to think about. And the carpenter's long muttered monologue — about tinkers and widows and cobbling versus clean jobs — is, underneath the comedy, an artisan's complaint about being asked to convert one meaning into its opposite. He'll do it, "tenderly." Thirty life-lines around a coffin, he says, so that if the ship goes down there'll be thirty fellows fighting for one coffin, "a sight not seen very often beneath the sun." He is nearly right about the number. He is wrong about the fighting.

annotations.quote: like half-articulated wailings of the ghosts of all Herod’s murdered Innocents
annotations.note: The first thing the sound reminds anyone of is slaughtered children, and it prepares us for the Rachel two chapters on, weeping for hers. The book's last movement is full of lost sons.

annotations.quote: In the sea, under certain circumstances, seals have more than once been mistaken for men.
annotations.note: The reverse is also going to be true: a man in the water will look like a sea-creature. Melville's flat naturalist tone here is a way of letting the horror in the back door.

annotations.quote: the sun having long beat upon this cask it had shrunken, so that it slowly filled, and that parched wood also filled at its every pore; and the studded iron-bound cask followed the sailor to the bottom, as if to yield him his pillow
annotations.note: The life-buoy that drowns with the man it was meant to save. Melville lets the safety equipment be as rotted as the log-line — nothing on this ship has been maintained except the purpose.

annotations.quote: they were not grieved at this event, at least as a portent; for they regarded it, not as a foreshadowing of evil in the future, but as the fulfilment of an evil already presaged.
annotations.note: There is a strange comfort in believing a bad thing was owed. The crew has stopped fearing the future and started auditing the past; that, more than any storm, is what fatalism does to people.

annotations.quote: Queequeg hinted a hint concerning his coffin.
annotations.note: One of the great quiet turns of the plot. Queequeg, who ordered his coffin and then decided not to die, now offers the thing he no longer needs. His whole character is in that generosity.

annotations.quote: Rig it, carpenter; do not look at me so—the coffin, I mean. Dost thou hear me? Rig it.
annotations.note: Starbuck can give the order but not meet the carpenter's eye, and cannot even say the word first time round. Six chapters from the end, he still flinches where Ahab does not.

annotations.quote: It’s like turning an old coat; going to bring the flesh on the other side now.
annotations.note: The carpenter's image for converting a coffin into a life-buoy — turning it inside out, death-side in, life-side out. It's the most exact description of what the object will finally do for Ishmael.

annotations.quote: not a cobbler’s job, that’s at an end in the middle, and at the beginning at the end.
annotations.note: The carpenter is complaining about patchwork, but he has accidentally described the book — a story that ends at the beginning, with Ishmael floating, waiting to be able to say 'Call me Ishmael.'

annotations.quote: Then, if the hull go down, there’ll be thirty lively fellows all fighting for one coffin, a sight not seen very often beneath the sun!
annotations.note: He means it as a grotesque joke. The reader who has finished the book knows there will be one fellow, and no fighting, and that the sight will be seen only by him.

links.why: Where the coffin was built, and why Queequeg decided not to use it.
The carpenter’s conversion of it, and Ahab’s speech about immortality-preservers.
What the coffin finally does.

ch127.essay:
Ahab and the carpenter, over the coffin, and I think this is the funniest and bleakest dialogue in the book. Ahab, who has just said "thy coffin lies handy to the vault" as a pleasantry, catechizes the man: leg-maker? undertaker? and now life-buoy maker out of coffins? "Thou art as unprincipled as the gods, and as much of a jack-of-all-trades." The carpenter's reply is the book's plainest statement of craft without meaning: "I do not mean anything, sir. I do as I do." Ahab hears it and says, "The gods again." He cannot stop hearing theology in a working man's shrug.

The bit about the sounding-board stays with me. The coffin lid rings when tapped, Ahab says, because there is nothing beneath it — and then, quietly, a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same. That's the metaphysics of the whole voyage compressed into acoustics: you can't tell the hollow thing from the full one by the noise it makes. Then the carpenter says "Faith, sir" as an interjection and Ahab pounces — "Faith? What's that?" — and the poor man has to explain that it's just a sort of exclamation. It is, and it isn't.

Ahab's soliloquy at the end is the one place he actually turns the coffin-buoy over in his mind as a hopeful symbol. "Can it be that in some spiritual sense the coffin is, after all, but an immortality-preserver! I'll think of that. But no." He gets to the edge of the thought that will save Ishmael and declines it, because "so far gone am I in the dark side of earth" that the bright side looks like twilight. The idea was right there. He is the one man aboard who cannot use it.

annotations.quote: Thank ye, man. Thy coffin lies handy to the vault.
annotations.note: Ahab's idea of a thank-you: the coffin is conveniently near the open hatch. He can't say a civil sentence without a grave in it.

annotations.quote: Thou art as unprincipled as the gods, and as much of a jack-of-all-trades.
annotations.note: Ahab's complaint against the carpenter is exactly his complaint against heaven — that it makes legs and coffins and life-buoys with the same indifferent hands. The carpenter is the nearest thing to God he can shout at.

annotations.quote: But I do not mean anything, sir. I do as I do.
annotations.note: The one creed on the Pequod that isn't a quarrel. The carpenter has no meaning to defend and so cannot be wounded by Ahab's; I find him oddly enviable.

annotations.quote: there’s naught beneath. And yet, a coffin with a body in it rings pretty much the same, Carpenter.
annotations.note: You cannot tell the empty from the full by tapping. Ahab has just said out loud that the universe's silence proves nothing either way about whether anything is in it.

annotations.quote: “Faith? What’s that?”
annotations.note: The carpenter says 'faith' as filler and Ahab treats it as a doctrinal claim. It's funny, and it's also the honest answer: nobody on this ship can define the word.

annotations.quote: Can it be that in some spiritual sense the coffin is, after all, but an immortality-preserver! I’ll think of that. But no.
annotations.note: He arrives at the book's own ending — the coffin as the thing that keeps a man afloat — and dismisses it in three words. The gap between 'I'll think of that' and 'But no' is the whole distance between Ahab and Ishmael.

annotations.quote: So far gone am I in the dark side of earth, that its other side, the theoretic bright one, seems but uncertain twilight to me.
annotations.note: Not that the bright side doesn't exist, only that he can no longer see it clearly from where he stands. It's a more honest self-diagnosis than any of the defiance, and it comes to him alone, listening to hammering.

links.why: Ahab and the carpenter the first time — the same contempt, the same competence.
Why the ship needs a new life-buoy.
The “cunning spring” going off.

ch128.essay:
This is the chapter where I stop being able to admire Ahab, and I am fairly sure Melville placed it exactly where he did so that it would happen to you here, seven chapters from the end, after the Symphony has not yet had its chance to make him human again. The mechanics of the scene are worth laying out, because the chapter is built as a collision of two searches. The Rachel comes down with every spar "clustered with men" — a ship that is all lookouts. Ahab's greeting is the one he has given every ship since [[ch52:Albatross|the Albatross]]: "Hast seen the White Whale?" And for once the answer is yes, yesterday. This is the news he has crossed the world for. Then the stranger asks his question — have you seen a whale-boat adrift? — and the two ships are revealed to be hunting different things across the same water. Ahab has to strangle his own joy ("throttling his joy") to answer. That verb is the chapter's thesis: which feeling is bigger in him.

Then the truth comes out in stages, and the staging is deliberate. Stubb's cynical guess — the missing boat had the captain's best coat and watch in it — is the reader's own cynicism, offered so that it can curdle when Gardiner says "My boy, my own boy is among them." Twelve years old. And worse, buried in a subordinate clause: Gardiner had two sons in two separated boats, the mate followed procedure and picked up the boat with more men, so the father has already, once, chosen the majority over his own child. Melville does not dwell on this for a second. He drops it and moves on, which is how the worst things in this book are told.

Gardiner makes the one appeal that ought to work: "For you too have a boy, Captain Ahab." We have heard of that boy only in passing, in [[ch16:you will no doubt remember|Peleg's account]] of Ahab's marriage, and we will hear of him again from Ahab's own mouth in [[ch132:human eye|The Symphony]]; Melville is setting up that later scene here, so that when Ahab weeps for his own child four chapters on you will remember that he had a chance to save someone else's and took it away. Gardiner even thinks he sees Ahab relent. He does not. "Captain Gardiner, I will not do it. Even now I lose time."

What I keep turning over is the sentence "God bless ye, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go." This is not madness. A madman would not need forgiveness. This is a man who sees the wrong perfectly, names it, asks his own forgiveness for it in advance, commits it, and then goes below with his face hidden. It is a harder thing to read than any of the speeches about fate, because the fate-talk lets him off and this sentence does not. If you want the counter-case for Ahab, it is in the previous chapter, [[ch127:the coffin|The Deck]], where he calls a coffin an immortality-preserver and half-means it; the man has a grim wit and a real inner life. But here the inner life is exactly what condemns him.

The last image is from Jeremiah 31 as quoted in Matthew 2 for Herod's slaughter of the infants: "Rachel weeping for her children, because they were not." Two chapters ago the seals cried in the night like the drowned; here a ship yaws after every dark spot on the sea, looking. And it is this ship, still looking, that will find the book's other orphan in the [[epilogue:orphan|Epilogue]]. I think that is the one act of grace in the whole novel, and it comes from the man Ahab turned away. Ishmael is picked up by grief that was looking for someone else.

annotations.quote: the boastful sails all fell together as blank bladders that are burst, and all life fled from the smitten hull.
annotations.note: The Pequod's canvas literally goes slack at the sight of the Rachel — as if the ship itself feels the approaching claim on it before anyone speaks. Melville often lets the vessel react before the men do.

annotations.quote: “Hast seen the White Whale?”
annotations.note: Ahab's greeting to every ship, and here it collides with a father's "Have ye seen a whale-boat adrift?" Two searches, two griefs; the book asks you to weigh them and makes the answer obvious.

annotations.quote: Throttling his joy, Ahab negatively answered this unexpected question
annotations.note: He has to strangle his own happiness to answer a stranger's anguish. The verb tells you which feeling is bigger in him.

annotations.quote: My boy, my own boy is among them. For God’s sake—I beg, I conjure
annotations.note: Stubb's jokes about a lost coat die mid-sentence. This is the only moment in the book where someone asks Ahab for something with a whole human life behind it and no metaphysics at all.

annotations.quote: the wretched father was plunged to the bottom of the cruellest perplexity
annotations.note: Gardiner had two sons in two separated boats and the mate followed procedure — pick up the majority. Melville hides this second grief inside a long explanatory paragraph, which is how real grief hides too.

annotations.quote: Ahab still stood like an anvil, receiving every shock, but without the least quivering of his own.
annotations.note: An anvil is the image from the blacksmith chapters — the thing the harpoon was beaten on. Ahab has become the surface his own weapon was forged against.

annotations.quote: For _you_ too have a boy, Captain Ahab—though but a child, and nestling safely at home now—a child of your old age too
annotations.note: The appeal that should have worked, and for a moment seems to. We will hear of this boy again from Ahab himself in [[ch132:human eye|The Symphony]], when he sees the child in Starbuck's eye — and Melville wants you to remember, at that moment, that Ahab had a chance to give another man his son back and refused.

annotations.quote: Captain Gardiner, I will not do it. Even now I lose time. Good-bye, good-bye. God bless ye, man, and may I forgive myself, but I must go.
annotations.note: Not madness — clarity. He names the sin, asks his own forgiveness for it in advance, and commits it. I find this harder to read than any of the rages.

annotations.quote: as three tall cherry trees, when the boys are cherrying among the boughs.
annotations.note: The Rachel's masts full of searching men are compared to trees full of boys picking fruit. The image is deliberately sweet and it wounds, because the boy they're looking for is not among the boughs.

annotations.quote: She was Rachel, weeping for her children, because they were not.
annotations.note: Jeremiah 31:15, quoted in Matthew for Herod's massacre of the infants. The seals two chapters back, in [[ch126:seals|The Life-Buoy]], wailed like murdered innocents; now the ship itself is a mourning mother. And it is this ship, still searching, that will pick up Ishmael in the [[epilogue:orphan|Epilogue]] — the one grace in the book, given by the man Ahab refused.

annotations.quote: Stubb to Flask, “that some one in that missing boat wore off that Captain’s best coat; mayhap, his watch—he’s so cursed anxious to get it back.
annotations.note: Melville hands the reader's own cynicism to Stubb so that it can be shamed a sentence later. Notice that Stubb, of all people, immediately reverses himself — 'We must save that boy.' Even the book's laughing man knows the right answer. Only Ahab doesn't.

annotations.quote: Avast,” cried Ahab—“touch not a rope-yarn”

ch129.essay:
The one act of mercy Ahab performs, and it's a banishment. Pip wants to follow him on deck; Ahab tells him to stay below, in the captain's own screwed-down chair, because "there is that in thee, poor lad, which I feel too curing to my malady." He is saying, as plainly as he ever says anything, that the boy's love might heal him and that he needs to stay sick. "Like cures like; and for this hunt, my malady becomes my most desired health." I read that and think of every person who has pushed away the one thing that could have saved them because being saved would have meant giving up the grievance.

Pip's reply — "do ye but use poor me for your one lost leg; only tread upon me, sir" — is unbearable and also the truest love in the book, offered by a boy the crew calls a coward. And Ahab, hearing it, admits that "Ahab's purpose keels up in him," so he stops the conversation: "Weep so, and I will murder thee!" He means it as tenderness. Whether it is tenderness I honestly can't decide.

Then Pip alone in the cabin, hosting imaginary admirals, drinking shame upon all cowards, and hearing "ivory" overhead — Ahab pacing. "I am indeed down-hearted when you walk over me." He has become the ship's keel, the thing Ahab literally walks on. On rereading I noticed the door: "neither lock, nor bolt, nor bar; and yet there's no opening it. It must be the spell." That's the whole crew's condition — nothing physically holds them, and they cannot leave. Pip is the only one honest enough to call it a spell.

annotations.quote: There is that in thee, poor lad, which I feel too curing to my malady. Like cures like; and for this hunt, my malady becomes my most desired health.
annotations.note: Ahab says out loud that he could be healed and that he would rather not be. It's the most self-aware line he speaks, and it's spoken in order to send away the cure.

annotations.quote: do ye but use poor me for your one lost leg; only tread upon me, sir; I ask no more, so I remain a part of ye.
annotations.note: Pip offers himself as a prosthetic. The book has made much of Ahab's ivory leg carved from a whale; here a living boy asks to replace it, and Ahab refuses the living material.

annotations.quote: Weep so, and I will murder thee! have a care, for Ahab too is mad.
annotations.note: He threatens the boy to stop him crying, because the crying is working. 'Ahab too is mad' is the closest he comes to solidarity — two madmen, and only one of them dangerous.

annotations.quote: True art thou, lad, as the circumference to its centre.
annotations.note: Pip is the circle to Ahab's point. In the geometry of the book, the centre is where the vortex pulls everything down; Pip, safe at the circumference, will go down with the ship all the same.

annotations.quote: What? neither lock, nor bolt, nor bar; and yet there’s no opening it. It must be the spell
annotations.note: Nobody on the Pequod is physically held. Pip, alone, names what holds them anyway.

annotations.quote: Oh, master! master! I am indeed down-hearted when you walk over me.
annotations.note: Pip hears the ivory foot above him and feels literally trodden. He has become the thing Ahab stands on, which is what he asked for, and it hurts exactly as much as you'd expect.

ch130.essay:
This is the chapter where Ahab stops being a man among men and becomes weather. He no longer goes below. He eats two meals on deck, lets his beard grow "as unearthed roots of trees blown over," and the night-dew beads on his coat and the next day's sun dries it. The crew moves "like machines." And he and Fedallah stand at opposite ends of the deck for hours, staring at each other without a word — "as if in the Parsee Ahab saw his forethrown shadow, in Ahab the Parsee his abandoned substance." I have never fully decided whether Fedallah is a person or a projection, and this chapter is the strongest evidence that Melville didn't want me to.

The central act is strange and, to me, deeply moving: Ahab has himself hoisted to the masthead in a basket so that he, not the crew he distrusts, will raise the whale first. And the man he hands the rope to — the one man who could simply let go — is Starbuck. The one who nearly shot him. Melville underlines it: "freely giving his whole life into such an otherwise distrusted person's hands." I think Ahab knows exactly what he's doing. It is a test of Starbuck's virtue and a demonstration of Ahab's contempt for danger at once, and it might also be the only way he has of saying he trusts him.

Then the hawk takes his hat. The Roman omen — Tarquin's cap removed and replaced, meaning kingship — is invoked only to be denied: the cap must be restored for the omen to be good, and Ahab's hat falls into the sea far ahead of the prow. Even the omens have started subtracting. And I love that the alarm comes from a Sicilian at a lower masthead — the crew is still trying to save him from small things while nobody can save him from the large one.

annotations.quote: As the unsetting polar star, which through the livelong, arctic, six months’ night sustains its piercing, steady, central gaze; so Ahab’s purpose now fixedly gleamed down upon the constant midnight of the gloomy crew.
annotations.note: Ahab has become the fixed point everyone steers by, and the crew live in his night. Having destroyed the quadrant that reads real stars, he has installed himself as the only one.

annotations.quote: Alike, joy and sorrow, hope and fear, seemed ground to finest dust, and powdered, for the time, in the clamped mortar of Ahab’s iron soul.
annotations.note: Not just fear is gone — joy too. A monomania flattens everything around it into the same grey powder, including whatever might have opposed it.

annotations.quote: his wan but wondrous eyes did plainly say—We two watchmen never rest.
annotations.note: Fedallah's whole role, if he has one, is to keep Ahab awake. I sometimes read him as insomnia itself, given a body and a turban.

annotations.quote: as if in the Parsee Ahab saw his forethrown shadow, in Ahab the Parsee his abandoned substance.
annotations.note: Shadow and substance staring at each other across a deck all night. This is the sentence that makes me suspect Fedallah is not entirely a separate person — a suspicion the book never settles.

annotations.quote: and then settling his firm relying eye upon the chief mate, said,—“Take the rope, sir—I give it into thy hands, Starbuck.”
annotations.note: He gives his life to the man who nearly took it. Whether it's trust, contempt for death, or the purest form of dominance — making your would-be killer your keeper — I can't tell, and it might be all three.

annotations.quote: Ahab’s hat was never restored; the wild hawk flew on and on with it; far in advance of the prow
annotations.note: The Roman omen requires the cap to come back. Melville gives us the classical precedent only to reverse it. Stubb's tarpaulin blew away in ch. 121; now the captain's hat. The ship is being undressed piece by piece.

links.why: Where the hawk ends up.

ch131.essay:
The last of the nine ships the Pequod meets, and the shortest of the encounters, and Melville gives it a name so cruel it's almost a joke: the Delight, carrying a smashed whale-boat on her shears and sewing a corpse into a hammock. "Hast seen the White Whale?" — "Look!" and the captain points at the wreck. "Hast killed him?" — "The harpoon is not yet forged that ever will do that." And Ahab, who has forged exactly that harpoon and tempered it in blood, holds it up and swears it triply into the whale.

What gets me is the timing. The Delight's captain is midway through a burial at sea — "may the resurrection and the life" — and Ahab shouts "Brace forward! Up helm!" to escape it, and cannot get away fast enough: the splash of the body reaches the Pequod, and "some of the flying bubbles might have sprinkled her hull with their ghostly baptism." A ship baptized by a corpse. And then the voice from the Delight's wake, seeing the coffin swinging at the Pequod's stern: "ye but turn us your taffrail to show us your coffin!"

"The rest were buried before they died; you sail upon their tomb." I read that as the book's summary of every ship encounter — the sea is the grave, and to sail is to sail on it. The nine gams have been, in order, a course of instruction Ahab refuses to take, and this last lesson is the plainest: here is what happened to men who tried, and here is the funeral, and you're interrupting it. He interrupts it.

annotations.quote: another ship, most miserably misnamed the Delight, was descried.
annotations.note: The last ship's name is a joke the narrator makes sure we get. After the Rachel's grief, Delight's grief — the names are running in the wrong direction on purpose.

annotations.quote: The harpoon is not yet forged that ever will do that
annotations.note: The captain means it as an impossibility. Ahab hears it as a cue, because he has forged one — the reader has watched it made and quenched in blood in 'The Forge.' Two men, one sentence, opposite meanings.

annotations.quote: the rest were buried before they died; you sail upon their tomb.
annotations.note: The four men lost without bodies were 'buried' by the sea itself. The idea that the ocean is already a grave you're floating on runs under the whole book and surfaces plainly here.

annotations.quote: not so quick, indeed, but that some of the flying bubbles might have sprinkled her hull with their ghostly baptism.
annotations.note: Ahab flees a funeral and is christened by the corpse's splash anyway. You can outsail a ceremony but not its water.

annotations.quote: ye but turn us your taffrail to show us your coffin!
annotations.note: The Pequod's escape reveals the coffin hanging at her stern. Every attempt to turn away from death on this ship displays it more plainly — the coffin-buoy is, literally, what she shows the world when she leaves.

links.why: The Samuel Enderby, the cheerful ship; the Delight is its opposite.

ch132.essay:
If I had to keep one chapter, it would be this one, and I want to be specific about why, because "it's the emotional peak" is not a reason. The Symphony is the chapter in which the book runs its experiment one last time under the best possible conditions. Everything that could soften Ahab is present at once: a perfect day, a kind sea, the one officer who loves him, an image of his own child. And he still cannot turn. If you want to know whether Ahab is a man who chose or a man who was driven, this is the chapter that refuses to tell you, on purpose.

It begins with a conceit that ought to be embarrassing — the air is a bride, the sea a groom, the feminine sky and the masculine deep — and it stops being embarrassing at the moment Ahab walks into it, "lifting his splintered helmet of a brow to the fair girl's forehead of heaven." Forehead to forehead, cracked against smooth. Keep that image; two days from now he will say [[ch135:Turkish mutes|forehead to forehead I meet thee]] to the whale, and the two moments are the same gesture pointed at two different worlds. Then the world, "the step-mother world, so long cruel," puts its arms around him, and he drops one tear into the Pacific, "nor did all the Pacific contain such wealth as that one wee drop." It is the only time in the book Ahab is on the receiving end of tenderness from anything but Pip, and notice he can only accept it as the kindness of a step-mother — as something not owed to him.

The speech to Starbuck is the most human thing he says, and it is full of arithmetic: forty years at sea, not three of them ashore, a wife married past fifty and left the next morning ("I widowed that poor girl when I married her"), a boy he has seen once. This is the boy Gardiner appealed to in [[ch128:my own boy|the Rachel chapter]], and Melville expects you to remember. Then the line I would give anyone who asked what the book is about: "let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God." For six hundred pages Ahab has demanded to see through the mask of the universe — [[ch36:pasteboard mask|the pasteboard masks]] speech — and here, for one paragraph, he says a human face is better than the thing behind the mask. He sees his wife and child in Starbuck's eye. He tells Starbuck not to lower with him. He is completely available to be saved.

Starbuck says the right things — exactly the right things, "let us fly these deadly waters! let us home!" — and Ahab's glance is averted, "like a blighted fruit tree he shook, and cast his last, cindered apple to the soil." And then the question: "Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm?" If the sun cannot move itself, how can a heart beat except by some other power? "Fate is the handspike." I go back and forth on whether this is profound or the most sophisticated alibi in American literature, and I have come to think that is the point: Melville wants both readings live and unbearable at once. The clue is in how the speech ends. It does not end on fate. It ends on hay — mowers asleep under the Andes, scythes rusting in the half-cut grass. He was reaching for a tender image, a smell of meadow on the wind, and what came out was a picture of everyone dead in the field. That is what Ahab's mind does to gentleness. Compare it with [[ch114:final harbor|The Gilder]], the other chapter that asks where the final harbor is; Ishmael, asking the same question, gets an image of a child's soul. Ahab gets a graveyard.

Starbuck, blanched, has already gone. When Ahab crosses to the other rail to look at his own reflection in the water, the eyes looking back are Fedallah's. After a whole chapter of Ahab almost being a man, the last image is of the thing that has replaced his face.

annotations.quote: the robust and man-like sea heaved with long, strong, lingering swells, as Samson’s chest in his sleep.
annotations.note: Samson asleep is Samson about to be shorn. The chapter's strength is dozing; the gendered air-and-sea machinery is elaborate, but this simile is what makes me trust it.

annotations.quote: lifting his splintered helmet of a brow to the fair girl’s forehead of heaven.
annotations.note: Forehead to forehead — Ahab's cracked brow and the sky's smooth one. Two chapters later he will say 'Forehead to forehead I meet thee' to the whale. The book is obsessed with foreheads as the surface where the inside can't be read.

annotations.quote: the step-mother world, so long cruel—forbidding—now threw affectionate arms round his stubborn neck
annotations.note: Not mother — step-mother. Even in the one moment the world is kind to him, Ahab can only accept it as the kindness of someone who isn't really his.

annotations.quote: From beneath his slouched hat Ahab dropped a tear into the sea; nor did all the Pacific contain such wealth as that one wee drop.
annotations.note: The hat is gone by now — the hawk took it — but Melville wants the slouched brim there anyway to hide the tear. One drop weighed against an ocean, and the drop wins. It's the book's least ironic sentence.

annotations.quote: wife? wife?—rather a widow with her husband alive! Aye, I widowed that poor girl when I married her, Starbuck
annotations.note: The cruelest self-accusation in the speech, and the truest. He knows exactly what he did to her; the knowledge changes nothing.

annotations.quote: let me look into a human eye; it is better than to gaze into sea or sky; better than to gaze upon God.
annotations.note: Ahab, who has spent the book demanding to see through the [[ch36:pasteboard mask|mask of the universe]], says a human face is better than what is behind it. It is the closest he comes to Ishmael's religion — the one worked out in [[ch94:squeeze|A Squeeze of the Hand]] — and he holds it for exactly one paragraph.

annotations.quote: No, no; stay on board, on board!—lower not when I do; when branded Ahab gives chase to Moby Dick. That hazard shall not be thine.
annotations.note: The order that saves Starbuck's life for two days and then doesn't. Ahab's one act of care for his mate is to keep him on the ship — the ship the whale will sink.

annotations.quote: But Ahab’s glance was averted; like a blighted fruit tree he shook, and cast his last, cindered apple to the soil.
annotations.note: Starbuck has just offered him Nantucket, wife, boy. The tree metaphor answers: whatever fruit Ahab had, it's already burnt, and this shudder drops the last of it.

annotations.quote: Is Ahab, Ahab? Is it I, God, or who, that lifts this arm?
annotations.note: The central question of the book, asked by the person least able to answer it honestly. Whether it is philosophy or alibi depends on whether you believe the man who says it, and Melville has spent six hundred pages making sure you cannot decide. The question has been building since [[ch109:let Ahab beware of Ahab|Starbuck's warning]] — 'let Ahab beware of Ahab' — and it will be answered, if at all, by a rope.

annotations.quote: we are turned round and round in this world, like yonder windlass, and Fate is the handspike.
annotations.note: The windlass is the machine the crew crank to raise anchor. Ahab sees all of them, himself included, as the drum being turned. The trouble is that he has spent the book being the handspike for thirty other men.

annotations.quote: they have been making hay somewhere under the slopes of the Andes, Starbuck, and the mowers are sleeping among the new-mown hay. Sleeping? Aye, toil we how we may, we all sleep at last on the field.
annotations.note: The speech was straining toward gentleness — a smell of meadow on a Pacific wind — and it lands on death anyway. Ahab cannot hold a soft image without it turning into a grave; the scythes left in the half-cut grass are the crew.

annotations.quote: but started at two reflected, fixed eyes in the water there. Fedallah was motionlessly leaning over the same rail.
annotations.note: He looks for his own reflection and finds the Parsee's. After a whole chapter of Ahab almost being a man, the last image gives him back his shadow.

annotations.quote: By the green land; by the bright hearth-stone!
annotations.note: Starbuck's oath is made of the two things Ahab has been running from for forty years — soil and a fireplace. It is the counter-oath to the one Ahab extracted in [[ch36:strike the sun|The Quarter-Deck]], where the crew swore on grog and harpoons; land and hearth against rum and iron.

annotations.quote: Fate is the handspike.
annotations.note: A handspike is the lever you push against to turn the windlass. Ahab has just said all men are turned like a windlass; now he names the lever. The image is so exact and so mechanical that I always feel Melville is quietly warning us against it — Ahab is very good at building machines that excuse him.

ch133.essay:
A hundred and thirty-two chapters of talking about him, and when he arrives Melville does the one thing I would not have predicted: the whale is beautiful. Not terrible — beautiful. "A gentle joyousness — a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness." White birds sit on the broken lance in his back like pennons; the sea draws a carpet for him; he is compared to Jupiter as the white bull carrying Europa, "the grand god." I want to insist on how strange this is. The book has spent [[ch41:maddens and torments|Moby Dick]] and [[ch42:heartless voids|The Whiteness of the Whale]] making the animal into a theology of dread, and now that the real thing surfaces, it is serene, and the serenity is real. Then the narrator warns: that quietude is "but the vesture of tornadoes." The calm is clothing; the storm wears it. That is the sea's whole character in this book — go back to [[ch58:push not off|Brit]], where the ocean is a lovely surface over universal cannibalism — and I think it is also what Melville suspects about the universe.

How Ahab finds him matters. He smells him in the night, "snuffing up the sea air as a sagacious ship's dog," before any lookout sees anything. Having smashed the quadrant, remade the compass and lost the log, he has finally become an instrument himself, and he has to be the one who sees the whale first — "the doubloon is mine, Fate reserved the doubloon for me" — so that the coin nailed up in [[ch36:strike the sun|The Quarter-Deck]] and read like scripture in [[ch99:doubloon|The Doubloon]] comes back to its owner. The pettiness and the grandeur are in one sentence.

The attack is horribly intimate. The whale rises from directly beneath the boat, seen first as a white spot "no bigger than a white weasel," then as rows of teeth, and takes the bow in his mouth "as a mildly cruel cat her mouse." Mildly cruel. Not enraged — playing. That is the horror of the first day, that the whale does not seem to be trying very hard. Ahab, who has spent the book making weapons — the harpoon forged and baptized in nomine diaboli in [[ch113]] — ends up grabbing the jawbone with his bare hands and trying to wrench it. It is the most direct contact he ever has with the thing he hates, and it is useless. Then the boat is bitten in two, and Ahab is in the water, "too much of a cripple to swim," his head "like a tossed bubble" at the centre of the whale's contracting circles, and the whole ship has to charge in to break the ring. On the floating stern, Fedallah "incuriously and mildly eyed him." If the Parsee is a man, that word is where he stops being one.

Two things on rereading. The paragraph about great hearts condensing "to one deep pang, the sum total of those shallow pains kindly diffused through feebler men's whole lives" is Melville stepping in personally to dignify Ahab's collapse — to say his suffering is an aristocrat's, concentrated where ours is diluted. I am never sure whether he has persuaded me or merely outvoted me, and I think that uncertainty is the correct response. The other is the speech at nightfall: Ahab claims the gold, re-offers it, promises ten times the sum divided among all if he raises the whale himself again. Even now he governs by wages. And "Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and ye two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone" — the loneliest boast in the book, and he shivers as he says it. I think the shiver is the true sentence.

annotations.quote: he suddenly thrust out his face fiercely, snuffing up the sea air as a sagacious ship’s dog will, in drawing nigh to some barbarous isle.
annotations.note: Ahab finds the whale by smell before any lookout sees him. After destroying every instrument, he has become one — a body that points.

annotations.quote: Not the same instant; not the same—no, the doubloon is mine, Fate reserved the doubloon for me.
annotations.note: He has to have seen the whale first, and he has to say so, and he has to invoke Fate for a coin. The pettiness and the grandeur are the same gesture.

annotations.quote: A gentle joyousness—a mighty mildness of repose in swiftness, invested the gliding whale.
annotations.note: After all the dread of [[ch42:heartless voids|The Whiteness of the Whale]], the first sight of Moby Dick is of something at peace. I think this is Melville's most daring choice in the ending: to make the monster beautiful, and then to make Ahab attack that beauty anyway. Everything terrible that follows is, on this first sighting, unprovoked.

annotations.quote: had fatally found that quietude but the vesture of tornadoes.
annotations.note: The calm is clothing; the storm is wearing it. It's also the sea's whole character in this book, and maybe the universe's.

annotations.quote: The glittering mouth yawned beneath the boat like an open-doored marble tomb
annotations.note: The whale rises from directly underneath, seen first as a white spot 'no bigger than a white weasel' and then as two rows of teeth. A tomb with its door open, coming up to meet you.

annotations.quote: In this attitude the White Whale now shook the slight cedar as a mildly cruel cat her mouse.
annotations.note: 'Mildly cruel' — not enraged, playing. The horror of this first encounter is that the whale doesn't seem to be trying very hard.

annotations.quote: he seized the long bone with his naked hands, and wildly strove to wrench it from its gripe.
annotations.note: Ahab, who has spent the book making weapons, ends up grabbing the whale's jaw with his bare hands. It is the most direct contact anyone gets with the thing, and it is useless.

annotations.quote: From the boat’s fragmentary stern, Fedallah incuriously and mildly eyed him
annotations.note: 'Incuriously' is a devastating word for the way a man watches his captain drown. If Fedallah is a person, this is where I stop liking him; if he's Fate, this is exactly how Fate watches.

annotations.quote: In an instant’s compass, great hearts sometimes condense to one deep pang, the sum total of those shallow pains kindly diffused through feebler men’s whole lives.
annotations.note: Melville intervening to say that Ahab's collapse is an aristocrat's suffering, concentrated where ours is diluted. I resist it a little every time and it works on me anyway.

annotations.quote: What soulless thing is this that laughs before a wreck? Man, man! did I not know thee brave as fearless fire (and as mechanical) I could swear thou wert a poltroon.
annotations.note: Ahab's verdict on Stubb — brave and mechanical — will be repeated the next day when Stubb says 'As fearless fire' and Ahab mutters the second half. A joke that has become a diagnosis.

annotations.quote: Starbuck is Stubb reversed, and Stubb is Starbuck; and ye two are all mankind; and Ahab stands alone among the millions of the peopled earth, nor gods nor men his neighbors! Cold, cold—I shiver!
annotations.note: The grandest isolation speech in the book, and it ends on a man being cold. I think the shiver is the real sentence and the rest is the coat he throws over it.

annotations.quote: and if on that day I shall again raise him, then, ten times its sum shall be divided among all of ye!
annotations.note: Even now Ahab governs by wages. The doubloon has gone from omen to prize to dividend; the crew is being paid, in gold that will sink with the mast, for the privilege of dying.

annotations.quote: tossed bubble which the least chance shock might burst.
annotations.note: Ahab's head in the water, at the centre of the whale's circling. For one sentence he is the smallest and most fragile thing in the sea, and the book that has made him a titan lets you see him as a man who cannot swim.

ch134.essay:
The second day is the one where the crew becomes a single creature, and I would ask you to read the paragraph that does it twice. "They were one man, not thirty." The ship is made of oak and maple and pine and iron and hemp, all welded into one hull; the men are made of the same diversity, all "directed to that fatal goal which Ahab their one lord and keel did point to." The rigging "lived," tufted with arms and legs. This is the most frightening paragraph in the book for me — more than the whale — because it describes something I recognize: the joy of being carried, of belonging to a will bigger than your own, and how that joy feels like freedom at the moment it is fate. Ishmael found this same oneness tender in [[ch94:squeeze|A Squeeze of the Hand]], where hands melt together in spermaceti and he wants to squeeze himself into everyone. Here the identical feeling is what kills them. Melville does not resolve the two chapters against each other. He lets you hold both. "Ah! how they still strove through that infinite blueness to seek out the thing that might destroy them!" — the narrator's one cry of pity for the crew, and it is pity for people who are enjoying themselves.

The fight is all tangle. The whale breaches, "salmon-like to Heaven," and then there are three lines fast to one animal, the boats hauled toward him by their own irons, loose harpoons corkscrewing up through the bows until Ahab has to cut them away with a knife. Everything the book taught you in [[ch60:hemp|The Line]] about how the rope runs through the boat is being cashed in. Stubb and Flask are dashed together "like two rolling husks," and the wreckage dances "like the grated nutmeg in a swiftly stirred bowl of punch." A wreck as a punch bowl. Melville cannot resist the festive simile even now, and it is exactly Stubb's tone — the [[ch49:desperado|Hyena]] laugh — surfacing in the narrator at the worst possible moment. That is the thing about this book that makes me love and distrust it at once.

When they count heads, Fedallah is gone, dragged under in Ahab's own line. "My line! my line? Gone? — gone? What means that little word?" The shadow taken by the substance's rope. This is the first half of [[ch117:the Parsee|the prophecy]] coming true: the Parsee has gone before. And Ahab's ivory leg is snapped again; that night the carpenter makes him a new one out of the keel of his wrecked boat — the same carpenter who in [[ch108:leg|Ahab and the Carpenter]] Ahab mocked as a soulless manipulator. He will stand tomorrow on the wreckage of his first attempt.

Starbuck's last real plea — "Impiety and blasphemy to hunt him more!" — meets "Ahab is for ever Ahab, man. This whole act's immutably decreed. 'Twas rehearsed by thee and me a billion years before this ocean rolled." Rehearsed is a theatre word, and the book has been a play since [[ch37:iron rails|Sunset]] gave Ahab his first soliloquy. He claims to be an actor performing a script written before the sea existed. It is the most complete statement of his fatalism, and I think the most self-serving; note that in the same breath he says "Fool! I am the Fates' lieutenant; I act under orders," which is a soldier's excuse, not a philosopher's. What I had not noticed before: he mocks omens to the crew and then, alone, admits the Parsee's riddle has him by the brain. He is up all night trying to solve how he can see Fedallah again. Tomorrow morning he will.

annotations.quote: the proverbial evanescence of a thing writ in water, a wake, is to all desired purposes well nigh as reliable as the steadfast land.
annotations.note: A whale's wake through the dark, tracked by skill alone, made as solid as coast. Keats's epitaph is 'writ in water'; here Melville claims you can read it.

annotations.quote: The ship tore on; leaving such a furrow in the sea as when a cannon-ball, missent, becomes a plough-share and turns up the level field.
annotations.note: The war-to-farming reversal of Isaiah, run backwards and sideways: a weapon that accidentally ploughs. The Pequod is planting nothing.

annotations.quote: They were one man, not thirty.
annotations.note: The oneness that Ishmael found tender in [[ch94:squeeze|A Squeeze of the Hand]] becomes, here, the thing that kills everyone. Melville puts the two chapters in the same book without adjudicating between them, and I think that refusal is one of the bravest things about the novel: fellowship and fanaticism are made of the same feeling.

annotations.quote: Ah! how they still strove through that infinite blueness to seek out the thing that might destroy them!
annotations.note: The narrator's one cry of pity for the crew in these chapters. They are hunting their own death with real eagerness, and he lets us feel both the eagerness and the pity.

annotations.quote: the odorous cedar chips of the wrecks danced round and round, like the grated nutmeg in a swiftly stirred bowl of punch.
annotations.note: A wreck described as a punch bowl. Melville cannot resist the festive simile even now — and it is exactly the tone of Stubb, who is at that moment bobbing in the water asking to be ladled up.

annotations.quote: Aye, aye, Starbuck, ’tis sweet to lean sometimes, be the leaner who he will; and would old Ahab had leaned oftener than he has.
annotations.note: Said on Starbuck's shoulder, leg gone. One of the few unguarded regrets he's allowed, and it's about not having leaned on people. Then he asks for a broken lance as a cane.

annotations.quote: _My_ line! _my_ line? Gone?—gone? What means that little word?—What death-knell rings in it, that old Ahab shakes as if he were the belfry.
annotations.note: Fedallah drowned in Ahab's own harpoon line — the shadow taken by the substance's rope. 'Gone' is the smallest word in the speech and the only one he can't get past.

annotations.quote: Ahab is for ever Ahab, man. This whole act’s immutably decreed. ’Twas rehearsed by thee and me a billion years before this ocean rolled.
annotations.note: Rehearsed — a theatre word. Ahab claims to be an actor in a play written before the sea existed. It is the most complete statement of his fatalism, and the most self-serving; compare the [[ch132:Fate is the handspike|handspike]] speech of the day before, where the same idea was at least asked as a question.

annotations.quote:
“As fearless fire,” cried Stubb.
“And as mechanical,” muttered Ahab.
annotations.note: Stubb echoes yesterday's compliment; Ahab finishes it under his breath with the insult. He has stopped expecting any of them to be more than parts.

annotations.quote: Oh! how valiantly I seek to drive out of others’ hearts what’s clinched so fast in mine!
annotations.note: He mocks omens to the crew and then admits, alone, that the Parsee's prophecy has him by the brain. The riddle he means to solve is his own death.

annotations.quote: of the broken keel of Ahab’s wrecked craft the carpenter made him another leg
annotations.note: A leg from the keel of the boat the whale destroyed. He will stand on the wreckage of his own first attempt to walk into the third one.

annotations.quote: salmon-like to Heaven.
annotations.note: The breach — the whole whale in the air. Melville compares the largest animal on earth to a salmon leaping upstream, which makes it, for a second, an ordinary creature doing an ordinary animal thing. The whale is not performing for Ahab; it is just being a fish.
