ch135.essay:
The third day begins with a lovely morning and Ahab's strangest speech, the one to the wind. "Ahab never thinks; he only feels, feels, feels" — and then he thinks, for a full page, about whether the wind is a coward for striking men without a body that can be struck back, and decides it is noble anyway, and asks it to blow his "keeled soul along." This is the most moving of all his monologues to me, because it is the first time he admires something he cannot kill. The wind is what he needed the whale to be: an agency with no body. He explained in [[ch36:pasteboard mask|The Quarter-Deck]] that he strikes the whale because he cannot strike the thing behind it; here, on the last morning, he finally addresses the thing behind it, and it turns out he can be gentle with it. Then "good bye, old mast-head" — moss in its cracks, no green on Ahab's head — and "this dead wood has the better of my live flesh every way." The farewell to the mast is more tender than his farewell to any man.

The chapter is built as a series of unheard warnings. Starbuck's handshake, "Starbuck's tears the glue" — and Ahab tosses the arm away a moment later. Pip's voice from the cabin window — "The sharks! the sharks!" — the boy Ahab put below to keep him safe, warning the man who saved him, and not heard. Then the Parsee's body lashed to the whale's back by the whale's own tangled lines, eyes turned toward Ahab: the first hearse, not made by mortal hands, exactly as [[ch117:two hearses|the prophecy]] said. "Befooled, befooled!" And he goes on. Starbuck's last cry is the one that stays with me: "Moby Dick seeks thee not. It is thou, thou, that madly seekest him!" The whale is trying to leave. Read the three days again with this in mind and you will see it is true: the whale is swimming away in every one of them. It has been swimming away since [[ch41:all evil|the first rumours]]. The whole hunt is a man chasing an animal that would rather not.

The ship is the second hearse — "its wood could only be American!" — and what surprised me on rereading is how much of Ahab's last speech is about the ship and not the whale: "must ye then perish, and without me?" He is heartbroken to be excluded from the wreck. "Oh, lonely death on lonely life! Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief." I would argue that sentence is the true climax, before the harpoon and the rope, because it is where he locates his greatness — in loss — and I think Melville half agrees with him and is horrified to. Then "from hell's heart I stab at thee," the dart, and the line catching him round the neck and taking him out of the boat "voicelessly as Turkish mutes bowstring their victim." The most talkative man in American literature dies without a sound, garrotted by his own harpoon-line — the hemp Fedallah promised, the rope [[ch60:hemp|The Line]] warned about, the log-line that parted in his hands in [[ch125:life holds thee|The Log and Line]]. Nobody sees him go. Melville gives the last word on Ahab to a piece of rope.

And then the paragraph I think is the greatest he wrote. Tashtego's arm still nailing the flag to the sinking mast; the sky-hawk — the same bird that took Ahab's hat in [[ch130:hat|The Hat]] — caught by its wing between hammer and wood; the ship going down "like Satan," which would not sink to hell until it had "dragged a living part of heaven along with her, and helmeted herself with it." Milton's Satan, dragging a third of heaven's angels down. Stubb wants a cherry. Flask thinks of his mother's part-pay. The three harpooneers go down still keeping watch from the mastheads, "fixed by infatuation, or fidelity, or fate" — three explanations, none chosen. "Then all collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago." Five thousand years is roughly the age of the world by the old biblical count. The book has spent six hundred pages insisting the sea is older, stranger, and more indifferent than any story we tell about it, and its last sentence is the sea not noticing. I always have to stop there for a while before turning to the Epilogue.

annotations.quote: Ahab never thinks; he only feels, feels, feels; _that’s_ tingling enough for mortal man! to think’s audacity. God only has that right and privilege.
annotations.note: He says this and then thinks for a page. The claim that he only feels is itself a thought, and a wrong one; Ahab's whole tragedy is that he thinks far too well.

annotations.quote: all the things that most exasperate and outrage mortal man, all these things are bodiless, but only bodiless as objects, not as agents. There’s a most special, a most cunning, oh, a most malicious difference!
annotations.note: The wind can strike you and cannot be struck. This is the clearest statement of why Ahab needed the whale — he needed an outrage with a body, something he could finally hit.

annotations.quote: By heaven this dead wood has the better of my live flesh every way.
annotations.note: The mast grows moss; Ahab grows only grey hair from ashes. His farewell to the masthead is more tender than any farewell to a person.

annotations.quote: Their hands met; their eyes fastened; Starbuck’s tears the glue.
annotations.note: Seven words for the last touch between the two men. Ahab tosses the arm away a moment later. The glue doesn't hold, and Melville knew glue wouldn't.

annotations.quote: “The sharks! the sharks!” cried a voice from the low cabin-window there; “O master, my master, come back!”
annotations.note: Pip's last words in the book, from the cabin where Ahab put him for safety. He is warning the man who saved him, and is the only one aboard who tries to call him back by love rather than argument.

annotations.quote: For when three days flow together in one continuous intense pursuit; be sure the first is the morning, the second the noon, and the third the evening and the end of that thing—be that end what it may.
annotations.note: Starbuck reads the three days as one day, which is how the chapters feel. He is the only character who narrates the structure of the book he's inside.

annotations.quote: Lashed round and round to the fish’s back; pinioned in the turns upon turns in which, during the past night, the whale had reeled the involutions of the lines around him, the half torn body of the Parsee was seen
annotations.note: The first hearse. Fedallah's prophecy fulfills itself in the most literal way — he goes before, on the whale's back, and looks at Ahab with dead eyes. Ahab drops the harpoon; it is the only time his hand fails.

annotations.quote: See! Moby Dick seeks thee not. It is thou, thou, that madly seekest him!
annotations.note: The whale is trying to leave. Starbuck's final, correct observation: none of this has ever been the whale's idea. Go back to [[ch41:maddens and torments|Moby Dick]] and you will see that even the rumours describe an animal that attacks when attacked. The 'malice' was always a reading.

annotations.quote: Ye are not other men, but my arms and my legs; and so obey me.
annotations.note: The last thing he says to his crew, and it's the frankest: they are prosthetics. Pip once asked to be his leg out of love; Ahab now takes everyone as limbs by command.

annotations.quote: “The ship! The hearse!—the second hearse!” cried Ahab from the boat; “its wood could only be American!”
annotations.note: Fedallah said the second hearse would be of wood grown in America; Ahab hears the riddle solved as the whale breaks the Pequod's bow. He is, at the moment of catastrophe, pleased to have understood something.

annotations.quote: Oh, now I feel my topmost greatness lies in my topmost grief.
annotations.note: The line I'd argue is the true climax — before the harpoon, before the rope. He locates his greatness in loss, and I think Melville half agrees and half means it as the last symptom.

annotations.quote: Towards thee I roll, thou all-destroying but unconquering whale; to the last I grapple with thee; from hell’s heart I stab at thee; for hate’s sake I spit my last breath at thee.
annotations.note: 'All-destroying but unconquering' — Ahab denies the whale even its victory. The speech is magnificent and he is about to be killed by his own rope, and the two facts don't cancel; they sit together.

annotations.quote: voicelessly as Turkish mutes bowstring their victim, he was shot out of the boat, ere the crew knew he was gone.
annotations.note: The most talkative man in American literature dies without a sound, garrotted by the line of his own harpoon — the 'hemp only' of [[ch117:Hemp only|Fedallah's prophecy]], the coils the book warned about in [[ch60:hemp|The Line]]. Nobody sees him go; the crew do not even know he is gone until the boat is empty.

annotations.quote: fixed by infatuation, or fidelity, or fate, to their once lofty perches, the pagan harpooneers still maintained their sinking lookouts on the sea.
annotations.note: Three explanations offered and none chosen. Queequeg, Tashtego, Daggoo go down still keeping watch — the book's kindest verdict on the crew, that they were faithful to something even at the end.

annotations.quote: went down with his ship, which, like Satan, would not sink to hell till she had dragged a living part of heaven along with her, and helmeted herself with it.
annotations.note: The sky-hawk nailed to the mast by Tashtego's dying arm. It is the same bird that took Ahab's hat in [[ch130:hat|The Hat]]. The Pequod ends as Lucifer in Paradise Lost, dragging a third of heaven down with him — and Melville makes the last living gesture on the ship an act of fidelity, a man still doing his job.

annotations.quote: then all collapsed, and the great shroud of the sea rolled on as it rolled five thousand years ago.
annotations.note: Five thousand years — roughly the age of the world by Bishop Ussher's count. The book has spent six hundred pages insisting the sea is older and larger than any story; the last sentence lets it prove that by simply continuing.

annotations.quote: must ye then perish, and without me?
annotations.note: Said to the ship. The most revealing clause in the last speech is 'without me' — Ahab's grief at the sight of the Pequod going down is that he is not aboard. He wanted to be inside the wreck he caused.

annotations.quote: Oh, lonely death on lonely life!
annotations.note: The one sentence of pure self-pity Ahab allows himself, and it is immediately converted into the boast about topmost greatness. Watch how fast he does that. He cannot stay in grief for a full line without making it a summit.

epilogue.essay:
"The drama's done. Why then here does any one step forth?" I love that Melville feels he owes us the question. He has written a book whose narrator vanished for two hundred pages into a voice that could not possibly have been in the room — inside [[ch37:iron rails|Ahab's cabin]], inside [[ch38]] Starbuck's head, inside the whale's — and now he brings Ishmael back, with a kind of embarrassed formality, to explain why there is a witness at all. I think the formality is the point. The book has been a play (Ahab said so in [[ch134:rehearsed|the second day]]: "rehearsed"), and this is the actor coming out after the curtain to explain how he got off the stage alive.

The answer is a chain of accidents, and the accidents are the argument. The Parsee vanished, so the bowsman moved up to Ahab's boat, so Ishmael moved into the bow, so he was the third man thrown from the boat on the last day and dropped astern. He survives by promotion up a ladder of the dead, by being the least important person in the last scene. This is what the whole book has been saying about Ishmael as against Ahab: Ahab is a centre and Ishmael is a periphery, a man who is porous, who [[ch10:cannibalistically|shared a bed with a cannibal]] and [[ch94:squeeze|squeezed hands in spermaceti]] and takes every subject in the world seriously in turn. Ahab has one meaning and is destroyed by it; Ishmael has all of them and floats.

The mechanics are precise and mythic at once. Drawn toward the vortex "like another Ixion" — Ixion, bound to a burning wheel forever for lusting after a goddess; Ishmael revolves on the wheel and, unlike Ixion, is let off — he reaches the centre just as the coffin life-buoy bursts up, released by "its cunning spring" exactly as the carpenter promised in [[ch127:the coffin|The Deck]]. Queequeg's coffin: built in [[ch110:Queequeg|Queequeg in His Coffin]] when he decided to die, abandoned when he decided not to, carved with the tattoos that copied a treatise on the theory of the heavens that no one alive can read, and turned into a life-buoy by the carpenter's blank competence after the Manxman heard the drowned crying in [[ch126:seals|The Life-Buoy]]. So the thing that saves the narrator is an unreadable cosmology carved on a box for the dead, which is also a fair description of the book you are holding. Ishmael floats on it for a day and a night. The sharks pass "as if with padlocks on their mouths," the sea-hawks with "sheathed beaks" — the same species that just ate a ship. Something has decided he is not to be touched. He does not say what. I have come to think the refusal to say is the most honest theology in the novel.

And then the Rachel — the ship Ahab turned away in [[ch128:my own boy|the Rachel chapter]] — comes back for her own missing children and "only found another orphan." I do not think the last word could be anything else. Ishmael is the outcast of Genesis, the son sent into the wilderness; the book began with him wandering to the sea because he felt like [[ch1:hats|knocking people's hats off]], and it ends with him picked up by grief that was looking for someone else. The thing that saves him is a coffin and the thing that finds him is mourning, and only now is he in a position to say "Call me Ishmael" — which means the whole book is what a man says after being rescued by the wrong ship. The epigraph is from Job, where four messengers arrive one after another, each the sole survivor of a different catastrophe: "And I only am escaped alone to tell thee." Escaped, alone, to tell. Three verbs, and each one is the whole story.

annotations.quote: “AND I ONLY AM ESCAPED ALONE TO TELL THEE” Job.
annotations.note: Four messengers say this in Job, one after another, each the sole survivor of a different disaster. The book lifts the formula of catastrophic news and gives it, once, to a man who took six hundred pages to deliver it.

annotations.quote: The drama’s done. Why then here does any one step forth?—Because one did survive the wreck.
annotations.note: Melville calls it a drama and asks his own question about the epilogue. The whole novel has been a play with a narrator who kept wandering offstage; this is the stage manager owning up.

annotations.quote: I was he whom the Fates ordained to take the place of Ahab’s bowsman, when that bowsman assumed the vacant post
annotations.note: Ishmael survives by promotion up a chain of the dead — Fedallah gone, then the bowsman moved forward, then Ishmael into the bow. He owes his life to being one seat further back.

annotations.quote: like another Ixion I did revolve.
annotations.note: Ixion was bound to a burning wheel forever for lusting after a goddess. Ishmael revolves on the vortex's wheel and, unlike Ixion, is released. It's the book's one act of grace and he compares it to a punishment.

annotations.quote: the coffin life-buoy shot lengthwise from the sea, fell over, and floated by my side.
annotations.note: Queequeg's coffin, the carpenter's despised cobbling job, the thing Ahab called an immortality-preserver in [[ch127:the coffin|The Deck]] and then dismissed. Built for one man's death in [[ch110:Queequeg|Queequeg in His Coffin]], it saves another man's life. The book's whole argument about meaning is in that transfer.

annotations.quote: The unharming sharks, they glided by as if with padlocks on their mouths; the savage sea-hawks sailed with sheathed beaks.
annotations.note: The same species that tore the crew and pecked the flag now pass him locked and sheathed. Melville does not explain. I've come to think the lack of explanation is the point — the sea isn't merciful, it's simply finished.

annotations.quote: It was the devious-cruising Rachel, that in her retracing search after her missing children, only found another orphan.
annotations.note: The last word of the book is orphan, and it is Ishmael's true name — the biblical outcast, sent into the wilderness. He is found by the ship Ahab refused in [[ch128:my own boy|The Pequod Meets the Rachel]], searching for a captain's son; grief looking for someone else picks up the narrator. I cannot think of a better last sentence in any novel.

annotations.quote: second day, a sail drew near, nearer, and picked me up at last.
annotations.note: A day and a night on the coffin before the sail; 'nearer' repeated is the only suspense Melville allows himself in the epilogue. The rescue is told in the plainest sentence in the book, after six hundred pages of the most ornate.
